title: Binary search trees: search, insert, build from a sorted array
overview: This module introduces the binary search tree (BST): a binary tree where everything on the left is smaller than the node and everything on the right is bigger. That one rule lets you throw away half the tree at every step, so search and insert take time proportional to the height, not the number of nodes. You also learn how to build a balanced BST from a sorted array by always picking the middle element as the root.

concepts.explain: For every node, all values in its left subtree are smaller and all values in its right subtree are bigger. The rule must hold for the whole subtree, not just the direct children.
Compare the target with the current node. Equal means found; smaller means go left; bigger means go right. Reaching `NULL` means the value is not in the tree.
concepts.snippet:
if (val < root->val) return search(root->left, val);
else return search(root->right, val);

concepts.term: Insert walks the same path as search
concepts.explain: A new value always becomes a leaf. Follow the search path until the child you need is `NULL`, then hang the new node there.
Search and insert cost O(h). A balanced tree has h about log2(n); a tree built from sorted inserts becomes a chain with h = n.
Take the middle element as root, build the left half into the left subtree and the right half into the right subtree. Both halves have about the same size, so the tree stays balanced.

concepts.term: In-order of a BST is sorted
concepts.explain: Visiting left, node, right in a BST prints the values in increasing order. This is a quick way to check that a tree really is a BST.

files.title: Search for a value in a BST
files.what: Reads a tree in level order (`-1` means no child), then a value, and prints `Found` or `Not Found` using the BST search rule.
steps: `input_tree` reads the root, then uses a queue: for each node taken out it reads the left and right child values and creates nodes for the ones that are not `-1`.
`search(root, val)` returns `false` when it falls off the tree (`root == NULL`).
If `root->val == val` it returns `true`.
Otherwise it goes left when `val` is smaller and right when it is bigger, so only one branch is explored per level.
`main` prints `Found` or `Not Found` based on the result.
files.complexity: Time O(h) for the search (h = height) · Space O(h) recursion
files.input_note: The tree in level order: root 20, children 10 and 30, then 5 15 25 40, then eight `-1`s for the empty children of the leaves. Last line: the value to look for (15).
files.output_note: You will see `Not Found` even though 15 is in the tree. That is the constructor bug described below, not a problem with the search logic.
files.watch_out: The constructor writes `this->val;` instead of `this->val = val;`, so every node keeps a garbage value and the search almost never matches. Fix: change that line to `this->val = val;` and the sample prints `Found`.

check.q: Searching for 27 in this tree, which nodes are visited?
check.a: 20 (27 is bigger, go right), 30 (27 is smaller, go left), 25 (27 is bigger, go right), then `NULL`, so the answer is Not Found.

files.title: Insert a value into a BST
files.what: Reads a BST in level order and one new value, inserts the value in its correct leaf position, and prints the tree in level order.
steps: `insert(Node* &root, int val)` takes the root by reference so it can create the root when the tree is empty.
If `val` is smaller than `root->val`: if the left child is empty, put a new node there; otherwise recurse into the left child.
If `val` is bigger: do the same on the right side.
Equal values fall through both checks, so duplicates are simply ignored.
`level_order` prints the tree with a queue so you can see where the new node landed.
files.complexity: Time O(h) for the insert, O(n) to print · Space O(h)
files.input_note: The same 7-node BST as the search program, then the value 13 to insert.
files.output_note: `20 10 30 5 15 25 40 13`: the tree is printed level by level. 13 appears last because it went 20 -> left to 10 -> right to 15 -> left, making it a new node on the fourth level.
files.watch_out: `level_order` pushes `root` without checking for `NULL`, so an empty tree (`-1` as the first number) would crash while printing.

check.a: So that when the tree is empty the function can make `root` point to the new node and the caller sees the change.

files.title: Build a balanced BST from a sorted array
files.what: Reads a sorted array and turns it into a height-balanced BST by repeatedly choosing the middle element as the root, then prints it in level order.
steps: `convert(a, size, start, end)` works on the part `a[start..end]`; if `start > end` the part is empty and it returns `NULL`.
It picks `mid = (start + end) / 2` and makes `a[mid]` the root of this part.
The left half `start..mid-1` becomes the left subtree and the right half `mid+1..end` becomes the right subtree, both built recursively.
Because the array is sorted, everything on the left is smaller and everything on the right is bigger, so the BST rule holds automatically.
`main` calls `convert(a, n, 0, n-1)` and prints the result with `level_order`.
files.complexity: Time O(n) · Space O(log n) recursion (plus the n nodes)
files.input_note: n, then n values in increasing order.
files.output_note: `4 2 6 1 3 5 7`: 4 is the middle of the whole array, 2 and 6 are the middles of the two halves, and 1 3 5 7 are the leaves. A perfectly balanced tree of height 3.
files.watch_out: The input must already be sorted; the code does not sort it. An unsorted array gives a tree that breaks the BST rule.

check.q: For the array `1 2 3 4`, which value becomes the root and why?

files.title: LeetCode 108: sorted array to BST

problem.name: LeetCode 108 - Convert Sorted Array to Binary Search Tree

files.what: The same middle-element idea as `array_to_BST.cpp`, written as the LeetCode `Solution` class working on a `vector<int>`.
steps: `array_to_BST(nums, start, end)` returns `NULL` for an empty range.
It creates a `TreeNode` from `nums[mid]` and builds the left and right halves recursively.
`sortedArrayToBST` starts the recursion on the whole vector, `0` to `nums.size() - 1`.
files.complexity: Time O(n) · Space O(log n) recursion
files.input_note: n, then the sorted array (LeetCode example 1).
files.output_note: Level 1 is `0`, level 2 is `-10 5`, level 3 is `-3 9`. That is the tree `[0,-10,5,null,-3,null,9]`, which LeetCode lists as an accepted answer. The middle index `(start+end)/2` rounds down, so on each side the left-middle value becomes the root.

check.q: Why is the resulting tree guaranteed to be height-balanced?
check.a: Each root splits its range into two halves whose sizes differ by at most one, so the two subtree heights differ by at most one.

files.title: LeetCode 700: search in a BST

problem.name: LeetCode 700 - Search in a Binary Search Tree

files.what: Finds the node whose value equals `val` and returns it; that node pointer is already the subtree LeetCode asks for.
steps: `search` is the usual BST search, but it returns the node pointer instead of `true`/`false`, and `NULL` when not found.
`sub_tree` walks the whole subtree and re-assigns each child to itself; it changes nothing, it just returns `node`.
`searchBST` returns the found node, which LeetCode prints together with everything below it.
files.complexity: Time O(h) for the search, plus O(size of subtree) for the extra `sub_tree` walk · Space O(h)
files.input_note: Tree values in level order, -1 for a missing child (tree `[4,2,7,1,3]`), then the number of searches and the values to search (the two LeetCode examples).
files.output_note: `searchBST(2)` prints the subtree `2` / `1 3`, matching LeetCode's `[2,1,3]`. `searchBST(5)` prints `(empty tree)` because 5 is not in the BST, matching `[]`.
files.watch_out: `sub_tree` is unnecessary: a node pointer already carries its whole subtree. `return search(root, val);` is enough.

check.q: Why doesn't returning the node lose its children?
check.a: The node still holds its `left` and `right` pointers, so whoever receives it can reach the whole subtree.

recap: BST: left subtree smaller, right subtree bigger, for every node.
Search and insert follow one path down, so they cost O(height).
A new value is always inserted as a leaf.
Middle element as root turns a sorted array into a balanced BST.
In-order traversal of a BST gives the values in sorted order.

check_yourself.q: You insert 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 in this order into an empty BST. What does the tree look like and what is the search cost?
check_yourself.a: A chain going right (1 -> 2 -> 3 -> 4 -> 5). Height is 5, so search is O(n) instead of O(log n).

check_yourself.q: Is a tree with root 10, left child 5, and 5's right child 12 a valid BST?
check_yourself.a: No. 12 is in the left subtree of 10 but is bigger than 10.

check_yourself.q: How many comparisons at most does it take to search a balanced BST with 1023 nodes?
check_yourself.a: About 10, because the height of a balanced tree with 1023 nodes is 10.

body: Here are seven marks, already in order. Find 40.

You know the quick way from Module 3. Look at the middle value, and if the target is smaller keep the left half, otherwise keep the right half. Three looks instead of seven, and with a million values about twenty looks instead of a million.
The trouble is the array itself. To add a new mark in the right place you have to shift everything after it along, and a linked list, where inserting is cheap, gives you no middle to jump to.

So ask a different question. What if the halving were built into the **shape** of the data, instead of being worked out from indexes every time? That is the binary search tree. It uses the same node with `left` and `right` you built in Module 17, but the values now obey one rule: for every node, everything in its left subtree is smaller and everything in its right subtree is bigger. The seven marks look like this:

Now searching is just walking down. At each node you compare once and step one way; the branch you did not take is thrown away, exactly like the half of the array you dropped in binary search. Two searches, one that succeeds and one that fails:
intro.trace:
search 40
  at 50 : 40 < 50  -> go left
  at 30 : 40 > 30  -> go right
  at 40 : equal    -> Found

search 65
  at 50 : 65 > 50  -> go right
  at 70 : 65 < 70  -> go left
  at 60 : 65 > 60  -> go right
  right of 60 is NULL -> Not Found

body: Inserting needs no new idea at all. Walk exactly as the search walks, and the moment the child you want to step into is `NULL`, that empty place is where the value belongs. A new value always arrives as a leaf. Here is 45 finding its home:
intro.trace:
insert 45
  at 50 : 45 < 50  -> go left
  at 30 : 45 > 30  -> go right
  at 40 : 45 > 40  -> go right
  right of 40 is NULL -> hang 45 there

            50
          /    \
        30       70
       /  \     /  \
     20    40  60    80
             \
              45

body: What is new compared with Module 17: there a tree was only a shape you walked over, and every traversal touched all n nodes. Here the shape carries the order, so one walk from the root to a leaf is enough, and the cost is the **height** of the tree rather than the number of nodes.

That word height hides the one thing that can go wrong. Insert 20, 30, 40, 50, 60, 70, 80 in that order into an empty tree. 30 is bigger than 20 so it goes right; 40 is bigger than both so it goes right again; nothing ever goes left. You get a chain, height 7, and searching it is a linear search with extra pointers:

That is why sorted input is the worst input for a BST, and why the page also builds a tree the other way round: take the **middle** of the sorted array as the root, the left half becomes the left subtree and the right half the right subtree. Both halves are the same size, so the height comes out around log2(n): about 10 comparisons for 1000 values instead of 1000.
One last check you get for free: an in-order traversal of a BST prints the values in increasing order, so if the output is not sorted, the tree is not a BST.

The programs below take these one at a time. `BST_search.cpp` searches, `insert_in_BST.cpp` inserts, `array_to_BST.cpp` builds the balanced tree from a sorted array, and the two LeetCode files are the same two ideas written in LeetCode's own shape.
intro.trace:
20 -> 30 -> 40 -> 50 -> 60 -> 70 -> 80
(every node is a right child: height 7)

walkthrough.heading: Watch it happen: inserting 13 into a BST
body: This is the tree `insert_in_BST.cpp` reads (`20 10 30 5 15 25 40`), and the value it inserts is 13. At every node there is exactly one comparison and one step, and the node being compared is shown in brackets. A new value always ends up as a leaf.
walkthrough.frames_title: Press the arrows to walk 13 down to its place

frames.label: The tree already obeys the BST rule: everything left of a node is smaller, everything right of it is bigger. Inserting must not break that.
Start at the root. 13 < 20, so if 13 belongs anywhere it belongs on the left - the whole right side is now out of the question.
At 10: 13 > 10, so go right. Two comparisons have already ruled out five of the seven nodes.
The left child of 15 is `NULL`. A search for 13 would stop here and say Not Found - so this empty place is exactly where 13 has to live.
Hang a new node there. It is a leaf, and every later search for 13 walks this same path and finds it.
Printed level by level that is `20 10 30 5 15 25 40 13`, which is what the program prints: 13 comes last because it is alone on the fourth level.

walkthrough.heading: Watch it happen: searching for a value that is not there
body: Same tree, and this time look for 35. A failed search is not a special case - it is the ordinary walk that runs out of tree.
walkthrough.frames_title: Press the arrows to follow the search off the tree

frames.label: Looking for 35 in the same seven-node tree. Nothing tells you in advance whether it is in there.
At 20: 35 > 20, so go right. The left subtree - 10, 5, 15 - is dropped without being looked at.
The left child of 40 is `NULL`. There is nowhere left to walk, and that is the answer: 35 is not in the tree.

Three comparisons to say no, because each step threw away a whole subtree. The cost is the height of the tree, not the number of nodes - which is why a tree built from sorted input, a chain, is the bad case.

find 35

  at 20 : 35 > 20 -> right
  at 30 : 35 > 30 -> right
  at 40 : 35 < 40 -> left
  left of 40 is NULL -> Not Found
